title: £500 in a card
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on an elderly care ward. Mrs Gill, 84, who you looked after for three weeks, was discharged home yesterday. Today a nurse hands you a card she left for you.

Inside is £500 in cash and a note: "For you personally. Thank you for being so kind."
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Keep the money and declare it on the gifts register.
options.brief: Declaring doesn't make a large cash gift acceptable.
options.detailed: Declaring is the right process for small gifts, but £500 in cash from a vulnerable older patient shouldn't be kept.

options.text: Suggest to Mrs Gill that the money goes to the ward charity, if she wishes.
options.brief: An alternative, if she wants to give something.
options.detailed: She may prefer this to having it returned. It ranks third because it should be offered as a choice after you've explained you can't keep it.

options.text: Tell the ward manager and follow the trust's gifts policy.
options.brief: Makes sure the gift is handled transparently.
options.detailed: The trust's policy will set out how to handle and record the gift, and the ward manager can help. It ranks second because Mrs Gill should hear from you.

options.text: Keep the money, as it was a personal gift.
options.detailed: This could be seen as exploiting a vulnerable patient's gratitude. It is the least appropriate option.

options.text: Contact Mrs Gill to thank her and explain you can't accept the money.
options.brief: Kind, and makes sure the money is returned.
options.detailed: A large cash gift can't be accepted, but she deserves a warm thank-you. Explaining kindly and arranging for the money to be returned respects her. It ranks first.

explanation.issue: This tests how you handle a large cash gift from a vulnerable patient, kindly and transparently.
explanation.keyDetails: The gift is £500 in cash. She is elderly. The gift is personal. She has already gone home.
explanation.reasoning: [E] returns it kindly, [C] follows the policy, and [B] offers an alternative. [A] keeps an inappropriate gift, and [D] keeps it undeclared.
explanation.competing: Some would tell the ward manager first. The key puts Mrs Gill first because a personal thank-you matters to her, and you can follow the policy alongside.

references.title: Identifying and managing conflicts of interest
references.note: Gifts from patients and the risk of appearing to influence care.
